title: Interchange, Scheme Fees, and Merchant Pricing

questions.question: On a card purchase, which party receives the interchange fee?
options: The card network that sets the rate
The acquirer that sponsors the merchant
The issuer of the cardholder's card
The payment gateway that formats the request
questions.explanation: Interchange is paid by the acquirer to the issuer: the issuer settles the purchase amount minus interchange. The network sets the rate and runs settlement but does not keep interchange; its own revenue is the separate scheme fees.

questions.question: Why does the fee engine store 1.80% as the integer 18000 rather than the double 0.018?
options: Parts per million keep every published rate exact, so the only rounding is the one HALF_EVEN step
Integer multiplication is much faster than double multiplication on every modern 64-bit CPU
The networks transmit interchange rates in ISO 8583 messages as parts-per-million fields
A double cannot represent percentages above one hundred, which some premium card rates exceed
questions.explanation: 0.018 has no exact binary representation, so a double rate is already wrong before any arithmetic. Parts per million make 1.80%, 0.05%, and even 0.0013% exact integers, leaving one deliberate rounding per component. Speed is not the reason, and rates are not carried in ISO 8583 messages.

questions.question: A merchant on blended 2.9% + 0.30 sees its customers switch from consumer debit to commercial credit cards. What changes?
options: The merchant's net per transaction drops because interchange is now higher
The issuer's interchange revenue falls because commercial cards are capped
The acquirer's margin shrinks while the merchant's net stays the same
The scheme fees rise because commercial cards pay a higher assessment
questions.explanation: Under blended pricing the merchant pays the contract rate whatever the card, so the merchant's net does not move; the acquirer absorbs the higher commercial interchange and its margin shrinks or goes negative. Under IC++ it would be the merchant's net that dropped.

questions.question: The table loader rejects an EEA consumer debit rate of 0.10% + 0.01 EUR. Why, when 0.10% is below the 0.2% cap?
options: The IFR forbids charging interchange on debit cards issued inside the EEA
The IFR caps a percentage of value, so a fixed part exceeds it on small tickets
EEA rates must be quoted with exactly two decimal places of a percent
The fixed part must be stated in USD so that schemes can compare across regions
questions.explanation: The IFR caps consumer debit at 0.2% of the transaction value. A fixed 0.01 EUR is more than 0.2% of any ticket under 5.00 EUR, so a rate with a fixed part breaks the cap for small amounts. Debit interchange is capped, not forbidden.

questions.question: Why does the engine compute merchant net by subtraction instead of rounding it from its own percentage?
options: Subtraction is cheaper than another multiplication and avoids an overflow check
The acquirer's contract defines the merchant net as the residual amount by law
Rounding the net separately would require the merchant's currency exponent as well
Independent rounding of all four parts can sum to one cent more or less than gross
questions.explanation: Each rounded component can be off by up to half a minor unit; rounding four parts independently lets the total drift from the gross by a cent, which a double-entry ledger cannot absorb. Deriving the last part by subtraction makes the invariant hold by construction. Performance is not the concern.

questions.question: A 25.00 USD monthly fee is attributed to transactions of 100.00, 37.77, and 2.00 USD. What guarantees the three shares sum to exactly 25.00?
options: Largest-remainder allocation hands leftover cents to the biggest remainders
HALF_EVEN rounding on each share cancels the rounding errors on average
Computing every share in parts per million before converting back to cents
Sorting the transactions by amount so the largest one absorbs any rounding
questions.explanation: allocate floors each share, then distributes the leftover minor units one at a time to the largest fractional remainders, so the total is exact by construction. HALF_EVEN only cancels errors on average over many values; for three shares it can still sum to 24.99 or 25.01.
